body: Sunday, June 28 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivered a hawkish pause at his inaugural June meeting, with the dot plot signaling a higher-for-longer posture. The 10Y yield sits at 4.37% (−8 bps vs 4W ago) while the 2Y has risen to 4.07% (prior close, +8 bps vs 4W), suggesting the front end is repricing rate-hike risk even as longer duration finds some bid — the 10Y-2Y spread at +31 bps is positively sloped but still flat by historical standards, and the directional divergence between front and back end is the story. VIX has surged to 18.41 (↑17.0% vs 4W ago), entering an elevated regime. The S&P 500 at 7354 (↓2.8%) and Nasdaq 100 at 29118 (↓3.7%) are under pressure while the Russell 2000 at 3010 (↑2.5%) is outperforming — a classic mega-cap de-rating rotation.

New / Most Important: The structural shift here is the Warsh Fed. This is the first chair transition in a decade and the signal feed confirms the hawkish tone is real — dot plot shifted hawkish, mortgage rates held near 6.5%, and there is active discussion about whether Warsh could actually raise rates this year. The Warsh Fed represents a philosophical break from the Powell-era "balance of risks" framework toward a more inflation-first, credibility-establishing posture. Markets are still adjusting their priors. The fact that front-end yields are rising while the long end is stable-to-lower tells you bond markets see this as credible hawkishness that will ultimately slow growth — a flattening impulse driven by policy conviction rather than panic. This week brings June jobs data and PCE — both are litmus tests for whether Warsh's hawkish stance gets reinforced or challenged. The wealth-concentration dynamic flagged in the feed (top 20% powering consumption, entirely reliant on equity prices) creates a reflexive vulnerability: hawkish Fed → equities weaken → consumption narrows further → growth slows → but inflation may not cooperate quickly enough to force a pivot.

Playbook ✓: Mega-cap tech selling off under rising rate-hike expectations is textbook. "Sell America" narrative being challenged per MarketWatch — US assets still attracting flows despite volatility, consistent with the structural dollar demand story.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The Russell outperformance (+2.5%) while Nasdaq drops (-3.7%) — Russell/Nasdaq ratio ↑6.4% vs 4W — is NOT what you'd expect in a hawkish-Fed, rising-VIX environment. Small-caps are more rate-sensitive and should underperform if the market genuinely fears hikes. This suggests something else is at play: either a structural rotation out of AI/mega-cap concentration into domestic cyclicals, or small-cap short covering on the view that trade/tariff risk has been priced. Either way, breadth expanding into a rising-VIX environment with the S&P falling is an unusual regime that historically resolves violently in one direction.

Macro Stance: The ECB has raised rates for the first time since 2023, reversing course after its easing cycle. Schnabel explicitly stated rates need to rise further to bring inflation to 2%. This is a paradigm shift — the ECB spent most of 2024-25 cutting, and has now reversed. Eurozone inflation remains sticky despite falling oil providing some relief, and Lane warned that inflation could stay elevated even with a peace deal (presumably Ukraine-related).

New / Most Important: The ECB rate hike is structurally the most important European development this cycle. This is a central bank that was deep into easing reversing course — the capital flow implications are enormous. The euro initially weakened to its lowest level in 2026 near 1.13 on the divergence with the Fed narrative, but has since found support. Bulgaria joining the euro is a sideshow but signals institutional confidence in the currency bloc. The more important signal is that ECB and Fed are now both hawkish — global liquidity is tightening from both sides of the Atlantic simultaneously, which is a deeply hostile environment for risk assets and EM capital flows. Foreign ownership dominance of the Ibex 35 (per the Spain article) highlights how dependent European equity markets are on cross-border flows that are now at risk.

Playbook ✓: Euro weakness on the initial rate divergence narrative was consensus. Eurozone consumers cutting inflation expectations per ECB survey is a modest positive.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The ECB hiking while oil prices are crashing (WTI ↓22.1%) is deeply unusual. Normally, collapsing energy prices give a central bank cover to stay accommodative. The fact that Schnabel is calling for more hikes despite this energy tailwind suggests core/services inflation has become genuinely entrenched in Europe. If the ECB is hiking into falling commodity prices, the implication is that the inflation problem is structural (wages, services, fiscal) rather than supply-driven — and that means the terminal rate could be much higher than markets currently price.

Macro Stance: The PBOC is rebuilding its operating framework rather than cutting. Loan prime rates were held for a 13th month in June (Reuters, [Jun 21]), the 1-year LPR at 3.0% (Mitrade, [Jun 21]), and the bank now plans an overnight reverse repo as the next stage of its policy shift (Bloomberg, [Jun 25]), with a survey pointing to a new overnight rate of 1.35% ([Jun 25]): the bias is easing, but the tool is liquidity, not price. The yuan fixing was weakened for a fourth session as the dollar advanced (Bloomberg, [Jun 23]): a managed drift lower against a dollar at 13-month highs, while the ECB openly calls the yuan undervalued (Reuters, [Jun 22]); T. Rowe Price sees it falling 1%-2% by year-end (TradingView, [Jun 26]). Prices are split. May CPI rose only 1.2% and missed expectations (China Daily, [Jun 10]), while factory-gate inflation hit a near four-year high on Iran-war input costs and the AI boom (Reuters, [Jun 9]).

PMIs & Activity: The official manufacturing PMI stalled at 50 in May (Reuters, [May 30]) with factory orders contracting (Wood Central, [Jun 1]), and the non-manufacturing gauge was barely positive at 50.1 (Macau Business, [May 31]). Private surveys were firmer, with services at 54.4 (TradingView, [Jun 2]). Industrial output growth quickened to 4.5% in May (China Daily, [Jun 16]), but retail sales fell 0.6%, the first drop in over three years (Il Sole 24 Ore, [Jun 15]), and fixed-asset investment was down 4.1% in the first five months (Macau Business, [Jun 16]). Industrial profits rose 18.8% in January–May (WSJ, [Jun 26]) and but profit growth slowed for the first time in six months as weak domestic demand bit (Times of India, [Jun 27]).

Credit Impulse: Total social financing grew 7.7% in May (CGTN, [Jun 12]) and topped forecasts (Bloomberg, [Jun 12]), but new loans missed as the property slump curbed demand (Reuters, [Jun 12]). The beat is government-bond issuance; private credit demand is still contracting. The PBOC is now urging banks to boost lending because demand remains weak, according to sources (Reuters, [Jun 26]). Household deleveraging continues (SCMP, [Jun 15]) against a $300 billion pile of bad consumer debt (Bloomberg, [Jun 17]). Read: the headline impulse is flat-to-positive, but the household and private-firm impulse is still negative, which is why output does not convert into consumption.

Property: New home prices fell at a faster pace in May (Reuters, [Jun 15]) even as first-tier new home prices rose for a third month (SCMP, [Jun 16]) and top-city resale prices extended their rebound (Caixin, [Jun 17]). Real-estate investment fell 16.2% y/y in January–May (GMK Center, [Jun 18]). This week the stress resurfaced at the developer level: Beijing land sales plunged 66% as developers chase only "safe" prime plots (Caixin, [Jun 25]), and the Evergrande Property Services stake sale collapsed, sending its shares down 24% (Caixin, [Jun 26]). Bloomberg describes steel entering a long plateau after the property crash ([Jun 21]).

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: The fiscal signal is the surprise. Beijing narrowed its cumulative deficit for the first time since 2023 (Bloomberg, [Jun 22]). A third batch of 62.5 billion yuan for consumer-goods trade-ins was allocated (Global Times, [Jun 26]): targeted support, small relative to the retail contraction. Exports jumped 19.4% in May (AP, [Jun 9]) and shipments to the US grew 35% (CNBC, [Jun 8]). The EU's deficit with China reached a record €1bn a day (The Guardian, [Jun 15]), and Brussels is hardening its stance as trade talks reopen (POLITICO.eu, [Jun 26]). Beijing hit 10 US firms, including MP Materials, with export controls (Reuters, [Jun 22]), and the 55% tariff on Australian beef is now in force (Australian Rural & Regional News, [Jun 22]).

Markets & Flows: Onshore and offshore have decoupled. Mainland stocks hit a 4-1/2-year high (TradingView, [Jun 22]), led by AI names on demand optimism and policy support (Bloomberg, [Jun 21]). Hong Kong is the opposite: the HSCEI entered a technical bear market (finance.biggo.com, [Jun 23]), Bloomberg ties the slide to spending woes ([Jun 23]), and the Hang Seng capped its worst week in over a year amid a tech sell-off (SCMP, [Jun 26]). Citi says beaten-down China internet stocks are worth buying on the dip (Investing.com, [Jun 27]) and PDD Holdings was flagged as a top non-tech pick, but with the Fed and ECB tightening together and Asia FX weak, the capital-account backdrop is hostile.

New / Most Important: Pressure for a policy response is building from inside. Government advisers are calling for a fix to the two-speed economy (Bloomberg, [Jun 27]), the same week the PBOC urged banks to lend into weak demand. With new loans missing and the first fiscal-gap cutback since 2023, the credit impulse that matters for households is not turning. The open question for the second half is whether Beijing reverses the fiscal tightening; until it does, growth leans on exports just as Europe prepares trade defences.

Playbook ✓: Property drag, weak consumption, LPR on hold and a managed yuan drift lower are all on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The consensus expected a mid-year stimulus pivot; instead the credit impulse outside government bonds is negative and the fiscal impulse is narrowing. China is therefore exporting its excess supply rather than absorbing it at home. The transmission runs through three channels. European exporters face record bilateral deficits and a weak yuan, and Brussels is no longer willing to absorb it. Bulk-commodity demand tied to construction is fading, with the steel plateau and an investment slump that hit AUD alongside the beef tariff. And global goods disinflation is the channel Pimco expects to support EM bonds (Bloomberg, [Jun 23]). A real turn needs loan growth, not bond issuance, to re-accelerate; until it does, rallies in Hong Kong are flows, not fundamentals.

Macro Stance: The BOJ hiked rates but the yen continued to fall — the textbook definition of policy impotence. Multiple BOJ members called for faster rate hikes, with one hawkish policymaker pushing for hikes "once every few months." USDJPY is eyeing 162, and an ex-BOJ official warned a Fed hike could push it to 165. Intervention warnings are escalating but the yen keeps weakening.

New / Most Important: This is the most structurally important yen story in decades. The BOJ is actively hiking into a weakening currency — a situation that fundamentally challenges the carry-trade mechanics that have underpinned global macro positioning for years. The government is now explicitly calling for "measured monetary management," which reads as political pressure to hike faster. But the rate differential with the US and now the ECB is widening on both sides, meaning the BOJ would need dramatically faster hikes to close the gap — hikes that the domestic economy likely cannot absorb. The yen problem is becoming a capital-flow vortex: Japanese investors hold massive foreign bond portfolios and as hedging costs rise (due to rate differentials), unhedged positions increase, which means more yen selling. Each BOJ hike paradoxically increases the incentive for Japanese capital to stay offshore because the carry is still massively positive. Intervention is the only remaining tool but it's a diminishing-returns game against structural flows.

Playbook ✓: Yen weakness despite hikes is consensus at this point.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The divergence is how hawkish the BOJ rhetoric has become — "once every few months" is an acceleration that could eventually snap positioning if they deliver on it in H2.

Macro Stance: The RBA held rates at its latest meeting but the tone is unambiguously hawkish. Hauser stated inflation "remains far too high," headline CPI cooled but core CPI stayed sticky, and bond traders are not ruling out a fourth rate hike. The lingering hike bets are keeping the Aussie dollar supported.

New / Most Important: The hold was widely expected but the fact that hike risk remains alive is the material development. Australia is now in the uncomfortable position of potentially hiking alongside the Fed and ECB — a synchronized global tightening that would be the most restrictive G10 monetary stance since 2007.  |  Playbook ✓: Sticky core inflation keeping the RBA hawkish is textbook.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: With WTI crude down 22% in four weeks, China's real-estate investment down 16.2% y/y in January–May and a 55% Chinese tariff on Australian beef, Australia's terms of trade should be deteriorating — yet the currency is holding up on rate differential support. This divergence can't persist; either commodity prices stabilize or the AUD weakens despite rates.

Macro Stance: A quiet Sunday on the data front leaves the picture from the week intact: the RPP is waiting (Parkiet, [Jun 25]), a hike vote was on record at the last meeting (Tysol.pl, [Jun 22]), and the NBP survey sees inflation under control with cuts uncertain (Parkiet, [Jun 24]). Disinflation is visible in the shops, where the pace of price growth is slowing fastest in food (Super Nowości, [Jun 22]), but Bankier.pl cautions that cheaper oil and gas will not free Europe from inflation quickly [Jun 24]. Growth is being carried by industry and defence: Business Insider Polska calls the jump in orders historic and the product of one programme [Jun 24], and Zero.pl says industry is drowning in orders [Jun 28]. The household side lags, with wages up 5.8% y/y in May below forecasts (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 22]), employment still falling (Bankier.pl, [Jun 22]) and Strefa Biznesu warning there is a catch behind the headline average pay figure [Jun 22]. Gazeta Prawna's forecast survey has the economy slowing in the coming years [Jun 23]. Poland is still described as the outlier dove in a hawkish world, but on this feed the right label is hold.

Markets: The week ended with Warsaw in correction mode: Friday's WIG20 fell with only Kęty and Żabka against the trend (Inwestycje.pl, [Jun 26]) as global equities sold off (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 26]). Friday's closes on the card: EPOL 38.27 (-3.7% 1W, -5.7% 4W); KGHM 327.75 (-10.3% 1W, -4.9% 4W) after the 7.5% slide on Wednesday (Portal spożywczy, [Jun 24]); Orlen 123.46 (-2.3% 1W, -12.6% 4W); PGE 9.6 (-1.9% 1W, -11.1% 4W); Allegro 37.19 (-5.7% 1W, +8.7% 4W) despite the buyback; CD Projekt 217.4 (-3.0% 1W, -4.7% 4W); LPP 18310 (-1.4% 1W, -16.4% 4W); PKO 103.62 (-1.6% 1W, +0.4% 4W); Pekao 228.8 (-2.8% 1W, -5.1% 4W); Dino 28.98 (-0.8% 1W, -6.6% 4W). The pattern is clear: four-week losses are concentrated in state-controlled energy, copper and LPP, while the banks are roughly flat and Allegro retains its monthly gain. FX: USD/PLN at 3.7661 (+1.4% 1W, +3.9% 4W) and EUR/PLN at 4.2788 (+0.6% 1W, +1.3% 4W), with the euro held under 4.30 zł (Bankier.pl, [Jun 26]) and bond yields falling as the dollar eased (pb.pl, [Jun 26]). Parkiet's verdict is that the GPW trades in the shadow of the zloty [Jun 25]. Debt-servicing costs are up almost 30% (Parkiet, [Jun 25]) and July retail bonds offer up to 5.65% (Subiektywnie o finansach, [Jun 24]).

Fiscal & Politics: The weekend brought no new decisions, so the standing items are the debt pile and the tax response. Public debt rose almost 47 bn zł in a month (FXMAG, [Jun 23]), wPolityce.pl puts May borrowing at 1.5 bn zł a day [Jun 26], and Bankier.pl warns of a coming accumulation of spending on nuclear and CPK with an EU procedure in the background [Jun 27]. The windfall tax sits between the Sejm's 60% (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 19]) and the Senate's 74% fuse (Wyborcza.biz, [Jun 26]). MF is preparing joint liability rules in property tax (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 28]), alongside the alcohol and sugar levies (Bloomberg, [Jun 24]) and the 2027 tax that routes around the president's veto on raises (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 25]). The CHF law awaits the president's signature after the Senate passed it unamended (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 25]), with automatic suspension of instalments on filing (CHF24, [Jun 27]).

Corporate & Sectors: Nuclear moved: the head of Westinghouse Polska said key elements of the EPC contract will be agreed in the coming months (wnp.pl, [Jun 28]), after Money.pl reported a dispute over the contract with the Americans [Jun 24] and Forsal.pl identified the 2036 completion date as the main problem [Jun 26]; the heatwave forced Hungary's nuclear plant to cut output over river temperatures (Business Insider Polska, [Jun 28]), a reminder of the grid stress that sent Polish spot power to 1442 zł per MWh (wnp.pl, [Jun 25]). Dino took a decision involving more than a billion zł (Portal spożywczy, [Jun 28]) and is closing one of its stores (Portal spożywczy, [Jun 28]) while its mobbing allegations reached prosecutors (DlaHandlu.pl, [Jun 26]). CD Projekt set the premiere date for Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 (PPE, [Jun 28]) after analysts cut the stock (INNPoland.pl, [Jun 25]). Orlen's fuel prices rose again from Saturday (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 27]). The Allegro buyback of up to 42 mln shares at a maximum 45 zł (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 26]) and the four-utility Ukraine letter of intent (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 26]) remain the live corporate stories, and CEO Magazyn sees Poland's software industry entering a more selective growth phase [Jun 28].

Geopolitics & Security: The warnings escalated in specificity: Poland's intelligence chief said Russia may use "little green men" in the Baltic states (Українська правда, [Jun 28]), NATO countries were warned of a possible Russian provocation against Poland and the Baltics (The Guardian, via УНН, [Jun 28]), and RBC-Ukraine reports an alert over Russian covert operatives [Jun 28]. This follows The Guardian's report that NATO leaders fear they cannot rely on US help if Russia attacks [Jun 27] and Sikorski's false-flag warning (The New Voice of Ukraine, [Jun 27]). Warsaw is also seeking to take over the former Russian consulate building in Gdańsk (The New Voice of Ukraine, [Jun 28]).

New / Most Important: The security premium is the story of the weekend. Two consecutive days of intelligence warnings about Russian provocations, layered on doubts about US backing, explain why Polish assets could not hold Thursday's bounce and why the four-week losers are all state-linked or cyclical. The offset is real but slower: a defence-order boom that Zero.pl says is drowning industry in work, and a Westinghouse EPC timetable that finally has months, not years, attached.  |  Playbook ✓: Hold-rate NBP; keep banks as the core long, stay light in Orlen, PGE and KGHM until the tax and security premia stop widening, and treat the Allegro buyback as the one clean domestic catalyst.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Industry drowning in orders while employment falls; a stable zloty and falling yields against escalating security warnings; Dino committing over a billion zł while its labour dispute is with prosecutors.

Macro Stance: Brazil's central bank signaled caution on inflation while India faces imported rate-hike risk from the US. Asia FX broadly weakened with yen and yuan under pressure. The dollar hitting a 13-month high and surging past 1,545 won underscores the hostile environment.

New / Most Important: The simultaneous Fed and ECB hawkishness is a dual-tightening vise on EM capital flows — this is the most hostile global liquidity backdrop for EM since the 2018 taper tantrum period. Oil crashing 22% is a mixed blessing: good for importers (India, Korea), devastating for exporters (Middle East, Brazil, Nigeria). China's growth pulse offers commodity-linked EM no offset: its official manufacturing PMI stalled at 50 in May and retail sales contracted.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: US-Iran tensions flagged in the feed could create a supply shock in crude that reverses the oil collapse — this would whipsaw EM positioning violently, hurting importers who have just been repricing lower energy costs.

Narrative: The consensus is a mega rotation out of tech: the Nasdaq 100 at 29118 (↓3.7%) is de-rating as Warsh-Fed hike risk lifts the 2Y to 4.07%, so rates, not results, set the multiple for now, with AI earnings the next catalyst.

Reported: BlackBerry lifted its annual revenue forecast as the QNX unit powered growth (BNN Bloomberg, [Jun 25]); Q1 earnings exceeded expectations and the stock climbed 20% (TradingView, [Jun 26]). TD SYNNEX beat on Q2 revenue and analysts raised targets (scanx.trade, [Jun 25]). Accenture's revenue-growth guidance cut shocked the IT services industry (The Hindu, [Jun 27]).
EPS Upside Watch: Oracle — a $638 billion AI backlog (24/7 Wall St., [Jun 23]) is contracted revenue still to convert into earnings, a cushion for estimates even after the stock's slide.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Tech is selling off while AI's economic impact accelerates — MarketWatch says AI is now firing up the economy. Improving fundamentals with falling prices is a rate-driven valuation reset, historically a buying opportunity, but timing is hard with a Fed chair hostile to multiple expansion.

Narrative: Meta and Alphabet drag XLC into the mega-cap tech de-rating in proportion to their weight, but the ad base keeps growing, with PwC seeing global entertainment and media ad revenue hitting US$1.4 trillion in 2030 (PwC, [Jun 22]).
Reported: No major reports this week.

EPS Upside Watch: Take-Two — an analyst says GTA VI could transform earnings (Benzinga, [Jun 24]), a single-title step-up in revenue and margins. Alphabet — Wall Street keeps raising its target while the stock slips (TIKR.com, [Jun 21]), estimates running ahead of the price.
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: Rising front-end yields (2Y at 4.07%) and a positively sloped but thin curve (+31 bps) are a workable net-interest-margin backdrop, and small-cap strength (Russell 2000 ↑2.5%) helps regional banks; credit quality is the swing factor, as Judo's bad loans show.

Reported: Jefferies' quarterly profit missed estimates as asset management weighed (Reuters, [Jun 24]), despite record investment-banking revenue (Quiver Quantitative, [Jun 25]). Australia's Judo Capital cut FY26 profit guidance after three loans went bad (Stocks Down Under, [Jun 25]) and the shares tanked (AFR, [Jun 25]).

EPS Upside Watch: Standard Chartered — upgraded by Deutsche Bank as the Asian wealth boom drives its earnings outlook (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 23]). Higher-for-longer US rates could also lift Singapore banks' earnings beyond 2026 (The Business Times, [Jun 25]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Financials leading while the VIX is elevated is unusual, since rising volatility usually hurts banks through wider credit spreads. Here the margin tailwind is winning, which says the market sees credit quality as intact — so further loan losses like Judo's would hit the thesis hardest.

Narrative: WTI at 69.23 (↓22.1% vs 4W) cuts upstream earnings while US drillers keep adding rigs, extending the downturn, and Trump's call for a DOJ price-gouging probe of oil companies (24/7 Wall St., [Jun 24]) adds political risk.

Reported: Worley, the engineering contractor to the energy and resources industries, issued a fresh profit warning (AFR, [Jun 25]). Oil-tanker earnings plunged by $200,000 as more vessels returned to Hormuz (Bloomberg.com, [Jun 26]).

EPS Upside Watch: BPCL and IOC — JP Morgan expects falling crude prices to boost Indian fuel marketers' margins, with the two set to benefit most (The New Indian Express, [Jun 22]): refiners gain when input costs fall faster than pump prices.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Oil down 22% in four weeks with US-Iran tensions elevated is counterintuitive, as Middle East risk normally puts a floor under crude. If tensions escalate without oil recovering, it would confirm the market sees any supply disruption as temporary against a structural demand problem.

Narrative: The small-cap, domestic rotation is the tailwind, with the Russell 2000 at 3010 (↑2.5%), as US business activity expands on manufacturing strength (Transport Topics, [Jun 23]) and lower oil cuts input costs for transport and manufacturing.

Reported: FedEx beat revenue and earnings estimates yet the stock dipped 6% (TIKR.com, [Jun 24]) as it warned on inflation and trade turmoil (Bloomberg.com, [Jun 23]). Primoris Services plunged after cutting guidance on renewables cost overruns, and its COO departed (Seeking Alpha, [Jun 22]). Bunzl upgraded its outlook (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: Southwest Airlines — UBS raised its target to $61 on the earnings outlook (Investing.com, [Jun 23]). IAG — boosted as analysts cut jet fuel cost forecasts (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 22]); cheaper fuel drops straight to airline margins.
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: Spending is K-shaped, with the top 20% driving it on equity wealth that is now falling, and guidance is the weak spot: beats are met with softer outlooks as higher costs and a hawkish Fed squeeze the mass-market consumer.

Reported: Carnival posted record $6.7B revenue but the Iran war cut its cruise profit outlook (Tech Times, [Jun 24]); shares dipped 5% on weaker Q3 guidance despite the beat (TIKR.com, [Jun 24]). Darden beat but forecast annual profit below estimates on higher costs (BNN Bloomberg, [Jun 25]) as Olive Garden growth weakened (CNBC, [Jun 25]). H&M profit missed estimates (Bloomberg.com, [Jun 25]).
EPS Upside Watch: Halfords — the UK retailer sees fiscal year 2027 profit near the top end of analyst estimates (Reuters, [Jun 25]) after margins hit a decade high (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 25]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Consumer sentiment beat forecasts while restaurant chains are closing hundreds of locations: the surveys capture the top 20%'s mood, the closures the bottom 80%'s wallet. That favours premium discretionary (luxury, experiences) over value names (quick-service restaurants, used cars).

Narrative: Defensives should draw flows with the VIX elevated, and falling oil (WTI ↓22.1%) eases freight and packaging costs, but pricing rather than volume is still doing the work, which limits upside.

Reported: McCormick topped profit estimates on higher pricing (Reuters, [Jun 25]) as organic sales grew (TradingView, [Jun 25]). Couche-Tard beat estimates on strong fuel margins (BNN Bloomberg, [Jun 23]), delivering its 'best performance in years' in the US, its CEO said (C-Store Dive, [Jun 24]).
EPS Upside Watch: None flagged; Constellation Brands' Q1 report is next (TradingView, [Jun 25]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.
Narrative: Defensives should draw flows with the VIX at 18.41, but a 10Y at 4.37% and a hawkish Fed keep a lid on multiples, while hospital operators such as HCA face reimbursement uncertainty.
Reported: No major reports this week.
EPS Upside Watch: Dr Reddy's — Nomura sees 35% upside after its strategic consumer-health pivot (The Financial Express, [Jun 23]), a mix shift toward steadier, higher-margin revenue.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Midjourney's entry into AI ultrasound scanners puts point-of-care incumbents such as Butterfly Network on the defensive. If consumer AI companies can build FDA-clearable hardware, med-tech's regulatory moat erodes — early, but structurally significant.

Narrative: Gold at 4096 (↓9.0%) and copper at 6.21 (↓3.0%) are both sliding: copper now trades on AI data-centre and grid capex, so its dip tracks the tech sell-off, and that demand case is not enough to offset a hawkish Fed.

Reported: Evonik raised guidance on higher prices and cost reductions (WSJ, [Jun 26]). UK chemicals group Synthomer beat Q2 expectations and its shares surged 8% (Global Banking & Finance Review, [Jun 22]).
EPS Upside Watch: PETRONAS Chemicals — Maybank sees 2Q earnings rising, though not sustainably as prices retreat (The Edge Malaysia, [Jun 23]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Gold down 9% in four weeks despite an elevated VIX and geopolitical tension is the starkest cross-asset divergence in the snapshot. It is put down to a hawkish Fed and easing geopolitical risks, but a drawdown that aggressive may be overshooting if Iran tensions re-escalate.

Narrative: With front-end yields rising and hike risk alive after the Fed's hawkish pause, mortgage rates have held near 6.5% for a sixth straight week (Realtor.com, [Jun 25]) and US new home sales posted a second straight monthly decline (Reuters, [Jun 24]), keeping rate-sensitive real estate under pressure.

Reported: KB Home beat Q2 sales expectations (StockStory, [Jun 23]) but reported lower revenue as a difficult housing market persists (WSJ, [Jun 23]). UK homebuilder Berkeley called for a tax and regulatory rethink after a 15% profit fall (Reuters, [Jun 24]).
EPS Upside Watch: Axis REIT — analysts call its latest purchase earnings-accretive at a reasonable price (The Edge Malaysia, [Jun 26]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: AI data-centre power demand is the driver, and Constellation Energy's long-term nuclear PPA with Walmart shows corporate offtake broadening beyond hyperscalers; a bill moving in Congress would make tech companies pay those energy costs (CNBC, [Jun 24]).
Reported: UK multi-utility supplier Telecom Plus fell 25% on its profit outlook and a dividend cut (Sharecast.com, [Jun 23]).
